NORML's Role In The Reform Movement: A Bright Future If We Stay On Message
Statement of Keith Stroup NORML Executive Director for the 2003 NORML Conference April 17-20, 2003 San Francisco

Introduction

Thirty-two years ago, when I sat around with a few friends and colleagues and put together the outlines for a public-interest lobby to work for the legalization of marijuana, we knew instinctively that this new group (then unnamed) should be a consumer lobby -- that is we should do our best to represent the interests of marijuana smokers.

Today, I am proud to say that remains NORML¹s focus. We unabashedly and proudly represent in the public policy debate those tens of millions of Americans who smoke marijuana responsibly.

I. NORML's unique role in the drug law reform movement.
NORML is a public-interest lobby that has for 33 years been a voice for responsible marijuana smokers. It is our responsibility to make sure that smokers are fairly represented in the public debate over marijuana policy; that the legitimate interests of smokers are advanced, including most importantly the right to grow your own marijuana, regardless of what legalization system is eventually adopted.

We lobby Congress and state legislatures, and we serve as a spokesperson for responsible marijuana smokers in the media. When others may attempt to compromise on important principles, and to pursue a strategy of appeasement, NORML must be the conscience of the movement. We must always do our best to make certain the interests of the consumer are met.

And while others may concede points for political reasons, NORML must continue to tell the truth publicly for all to hear: There is absolutely nothing wrong with the responsible use of marijuana by adults. There is nothing wrong with smoking marijuana.

II. I wish this were not the case, but NORML is the marijuana law reform organization that does not enjoy the financial beneficence of a billionaire.

That's one way to keep us straight from some of the other drug law reform organizations, notably the Drug Policy Alliance and the Marijuana Policy Project. Comparatively speaking, we are the poor folks, who represent the interests of average smokers, not billionaires. So we have to do our work the old fashioned way: we have to raise our funding from ordinary folks, a few bucks at a time.

That's bad news, as fundraising is always difficult and especially so with the stock market in the tank, and the country on a war footing. And the lack of adequate funding precludes NORML from undertaking some of the work that we should be doing.

But it also has its advantages.

We do not have to worry, for example, that a billionaire funder is going to force his will on the organization, or shape our programs to suit his particular ideas. Because we don't depend on some billionaire¹s funding, we have the freedom to do what our board of directors believes is right.

NORML must use that freedom to make sure that consumers -- marijuana smokers -- define the issue, establish our political goals, and craft the best solutions for meeting the legitimate needs of the millions of Americans who smoke marijuana. Only consumers can or should make those decisions.

III. However, while we may lack the bankroll of some other groups, NORML is the one drug law reform organization with a national reputation, the result of our having worked for 33 years to legalize marijuana. In essence, NORML owns the Coca-cola brand name in the drug law reform field.

In a Zogby poll commissioned by the NORML Foundation about one year ago, we asked how many Americans knew the name NORML and knew what we stand for; and we further asked whether the public had a favorable or an unfavorable impression of the organization.

The results: First, 24%of the entire American public claim to know NORML and who we are. That is quite extraordinary, in a world where half of the people cannot name the vice-president!

Second, 41% of the public have a generally favorable impression of NORML, while 47% have a generally unfavorable impression. While I wish this were higher, that's not so bad when one considers that NORML has been sitting atop the legalization movement -- a most controversial issue for most Americans -- for 33 years.

Third, and most importantly, of those tens of millions of Americans who smoke marijuana, NORML enjoys an 87% favorable rating! That reservoir of goodwill that has accumulated over the years is our most valuable asset, and it provides NORML with the ability to engage and activate our natural constituency in a manner which few other reform organization can do.

NORML is the principal lobby for marijuana smokers in America, and the marijuana smokers know that and appreciate it.

IV. The several reform organizations that work on marijuana policy must learn to work cooperatively on projects of mutual interest.

I believe very strongly that the various drug law reform groups who compete for funding and public support must learn to work more cooperatively. That includes most specifically NORML, MPP and DPA, three groups that have generally worked independent of each other, even when we agree on ultimate policy goals.

Specifically, we must learn to regularly share information; discuss and analyze strategy; vet each other's projects, and use our limited resources more effectively. Currently we are not doing this.

I was dismayed earlier this year when I attempted to schedule a meeting with our counterparts at MPP, for example, to discuss state legislative work -- an area where both groups are working, sometimes duplicating efforts. I was told that no one at MPP was interested in pursuing those conversations. This is truly an example of letting our organizational egos get in the way of achieving our common goals and does a disservice to our overall movement.

If we are serious about our work, this internecine posturing must end, and we must find a way to work cooperatively.

V. We must also be willing to acknowledge when we make mistakes, and to learn from those mistakes. Our political defeats at the ballot box in November of 2002 were largely of our own making. As a movement, we made some strategic mistakes that arguably doomed the initiatives in both Nevada and Arizona from the outset. By including provisions in those initiatives that clearly do not (and we knew this going in) enjoy majority support, we made ourselves easy targets.

In Nevada, provisions were included that would have required the state to establish a legally regulated market! Now, I like this idea, and NORML certainly supports legalizing marijuana. But every poll taken for the last half-century demonstrate that we do not yet enjoy majority support for legalization. Pre-initiative polling indicated 41% of Nevadans would support the proposed language in the initiative; not surprisingly, in the election, the reform proposal picked up 41% of the vote.
See
Their Liars Beat Our Liars. Freedom Has Nothing to Fear from the Truth, But Much To Fear From Those Who Think That the End Justifies The Means. Analysis By Richard Cowan


By including a provision that could never have been implemented anyway -- that is, until federal law is amended, states are not free to legalize marijuana -- the sponsors of the initiative essentially assured the measure would be defeated -- and it was, resoundingly.

The experience in Arizona was similar. The sponsors sought to decriminalize small amounts of marijuana, and to revise their medical use law previously passed to make it more workable. These provisions might well have won majority approval of the voters. But the sponsors also include some extraneous provisions that would have required the state police to distribute confiscated marijuana for free to qualified patients! That is counterintuitive on its face.

First, no other medicine is free in this country, and it is not smart to ask for special privileges for medical marijuana users. Secondly, if medical marijuana were to be distributed by the state, it should be done by public health officials, not the police. The provision was especially offensive to the law enforcement community, and caused an outrage of opposition.

Again, by including provisions that do not enjoy majority support, the sponsors assured the defeat of their own initiative. Could the defeats in Nevada and Arizona have been avoided if the sponsors worked in a cooperative and collective effort with other drug law reform groups? Possibly. I sincerely believe that if the groups did work more closely, the likelihood of making a strategic mistake, or wasting scarce movement resources, would be greatly reduced.

VI. There are serious repercussions when we lose elections.

Our opponents take advantage of these openings. The Drug Czar is now running around the country telling anyone who will listen that the American people have spoken, and they have rejected the ³normalization² of drug use. Our opponents now clearly have, in the short run, bragging rights, and they are hammering us in Op-eds and in other forums all across the country.

We have lost the momentum that had been built up with a string of victories starting in 1996, and the media no longer see our movement as being on a roll. In fact, many marijuana-related articles now include mention of the series of initiative losses we suffered in the 2002 elections.

So let's be honest. It does matter whether we win or lose these various battles we take on. When one group gets carried away and mounts a high-profile losing effort, all of us in the reform movement are harmed, even though most of us were never consulted or involved in the decisions that led to the defeat.

VII . Nevertheless, despite our setbacks last November, current polling data demonstrate we now enjoy the highest levels of public support we have ever had.

72% of the American public, nearly 3 out of 4 of our citizens, now favor a fine-only for recreational marijuana users, and 80% of the public support legalizing marijuana for medical use. (Support for outright legalization of
marijuana is also on the rise; now at 35% -- up 15 percentage points in the last 2 years.)
See
Democracy, Cannabis and the Drug Czar. Arrests Remain Close to Record Levels. Support for Medical Cannabis Now Up to 80%. And 34% Favor Full Legalization. We Are Winning, But The People Are Suffering.

So we have an enormous reservoir of support that we can now leverage, if we are willing to drop the cute provisions, take it a step at a time, and stay within the parameters where we enjoy majority support.

NORML, and the entire reform community, have a bright future, if we stay on message, and that message should be: Stop arresting marijuana smokers, regardless of whether the individual is using marijuana as a medicine or smoking it for personal pleasure or intellectual growth.

Our challenge is now less to educate the public, which is already largely on our side, and more to convert this public support into public policy. Primarily this means we have to convince state and federal elected officials that they will not be punished by the voters for supporting reform legislation. Over time, we must be able to demonstrate that voters appreciate and support elected officials who are willing to deal honestly and rationally with marijuana policy.

That means that our natural constituency -- the tens of millions of Americans who smoke marijuana responsibly -- must become more politically active. We must demonstrate that those who support marijuana law reform are willing to vote for candidates who support our positions, and against candidates who continue to support policies that treat smokers like criminals.

VIII. Nothing breeds success like success. Momentum, and the public perception of momentum, are important. When we win a state initiative, or pass a reform bill through a state legislature, that fact gives added support to marijuana law reform efforts all across the country. When we lose, especially statewide initiatives, the reverse is true.

So let¹s see if we can reach a consensus that winning each and every individual political battle is important, and that it is disruptive and self-defeating to the larger reform movement to initiate projects that are likely to fail.

Money talks, and those with the resources get to decide how they will spend their money. We all accept that reality. But they should begin to do that with a more realistic view of the potential damage a serious defeat may cause to the broader drug law reform movement. And they need to consult with a range of experts in the movement -- to have their proposal fully vetted by others -- to avoid the situation we ended up with in Alaska a couple of years ago, and in Nevada and Arizona in 2002.

IX. Summary

In summary, we enjoy stronger support from the public today than we have ever experienced, yet we still do not have the political power to move a simple decriminalization bill through a state legislature. In fact, with the exception of Hawaii two years ago, we can't even get a medical use bill approved by a state legislature. The bill that passed in Maryland, and is expected to be signed by the governor later this month, was compromised to the point that it is largely symbolic.
See
Is The War On Cannabis A Cult? Taking Cannabiphobia To New Depths Of Absurdity. A Method to Their Madness?

So where do we go from here?

First, we must insist that reform legislation proposed by those who claim to be our friends meet certain minimal qualifications. The legislation must seek to achieve basic goals supported by a majority of the reform movement, and must not undermine those goals strategically.

And second, we must be more thoughtful and strategic in selecting our political projects, legislative proposals and voter initiatives in the coming months. Before last November, the reform movement was on a roll. We were properly perceived by the media, and by the public, as being on a successful path towards nationwide reform. Since last November, the reform movement has been defeated in high-profile initiatives in Nevada, Arizona, and Ohio. The government is now (correctly) perceived as having the upper hand in these battles. This will be a significant burden that will hurt our movement and discourage citizens from joining our campaign until we can find a way to overcome this streak of losses.

In the end, what is important is that we continue to speak the truth; that we speak truth to power, regardless of the timidity of our elected officials. Eventually elected officials in this country will follow the lead of their constituents, and do the right thing.

Until that occurs, I would rather stand for principle, even if we cannot yet pass effective legislation, or win meaningful voter initiates, than I would compromise our goals for the sake of claiming empty political or legislative victories.

It is time we stopped arresting responsible marijuana smokers, regardless of whether they smoke for medical reasons or for pleasure, and anything short of that is a compromise I am unwilling to accept.
